data.about: Three trusses, no loads and no dimensions — the whole question is whether each one has exactly as many bars as it needs. The rule is a count: members plus reaction components against twice the number of joints. Too few and it is a mechanism that will move; too many and it is over-determined, and the forces in it depend on how it was built rather than only on the load. Step through and watch the tally build up bar by bar.

steps.caption: EX 6 task 1: three form diagrams, and one question about each — is it statically determinate?
steps.title: The exercise

steps.caption: count three things. S, the number of members. A, the number of reaction COMPONENTS a support can deliver — two for a pin, one for a roller. K, the number of joints. Then compare S + A against 2K
steps.title: The rule

steps.caption: equilateral triangles all the way along, a pin at one end and a roller at the other. Count it: eleven members, three reaction components, seven joints
steps.title: A — the Warren truss

steps.caption: more complicated to look at, and exactly the same answer. Its right-hand support is a roller on a plane inclined at 45°, which still contributes only ONE reaction component
steps.title: B — the stepped truss

steps.caption: this one is different. Each panel carries two crossing diagonals, and they cross WITHOUT a joint — so each panel has one more bar than it needs to be rigid
steps.title: C — the X-braced panels

steps.caption: not that it will fall down — the opposite. It stands up in more ways than statics alone can decide, so the forces depend on stiffness and on how it was assembled. Graphic statics can no longer give you a unique answer
steps.title: What over-determined means
